description: Which verification providers exist, what each one can actually observe, what it costs and touches to run, and the deterministic policy that picks between them (gh issue #8, epic #1; RFC 0001 section 8). A provider never decides a control. It produces scoped Evidence and an assessor decides, so selection ranks methods by the strength of the observation they can make rather than by how confident their output sounds. The strongest method is also frequently the most intrusive one, which is why every capability states its authorization, credentials, network and data-egress behaviour, side effects and cost: a provider the user has not authorized is excluded, and the exclusion is recorded as a coverage gap rather than passed over in silence.

executor_roles.automation: A bundled or installed program runs unattended once it has been authorized.
executor_roles.founder: The application owner performs documented steps and records what they saw.
executor_roles.developer: Someone who can read the application's source and configuration performs the check.
executor_roles.specialist: A security or domain specialist is required; the method is not safe or meaningful without one.

static_pattern_scan.description: Regex and path heuristics over a working tree.

code_review_of_diff.description: A human reads the source or a change to it.

migration_analysis.description: Statement recognition over committed database migrations.

policy_source_review.description: A human reads the declared authorization policies as written.

http_select_anon_head.description: A read request to the deployed backend holding only what a browser has.

http_insert_anon.description: A write request to the deployed backend holding only what a browser has.

http_select_authenticated_cross_account.description: A read of one account's record using another account's session.

browser_two_account_flow.description: A scripted browser drives the real application as two different accounts.

guided_browser_check.description: A person drives the real application as two different accounts and records the result.

live_http_response_inspection.description: The deployed application's own responses, headers and error pages are read back.

git_history_scan.description: Pattern and entropy matching over committed history, including commits whose content was later removed from the working tree.

dependency_audit.description: Declared dependency versions, lockfiles or image layers are matched against advisory databases. It reads what the project declares, never what the deployment is running.

sast_code_scan.description: Rule-based or dataflow static analysis over source code.

dast_web_scan.description: A scanner sends requests to a deployed application and reads what comes back.

operations.kind_rule: A source operation reads what the application intends; a live operation reads what the deployment does. Only a live operation may fill an authorization coverage cell, because an unapplied or dashboard-overridden policy looks exactly like an applied one in the source (RFC 0001 section 6.4). The source set here is the same set scripts/authz.py refuses a cell to.
operations.default_rule: A coverage entry that does not state fills_coverage_cell is read as filling one exactly when every operation it names is live and the control is coverage-tracked. The explicit flag is for the cases the default gets wrong in the unsafe direction: a live method that still cannot settle a cell, such as a browser flow asserting on the routes somebody wrote tests for while the control speaks about every route. An unrecognized operation is not a live one.

network.description: The provider sends a request to something outside this machine.
network.prompt_en: allowed to make network requests to the target

data_egress.description: Application or user data leaves this machine as part of running the check.
data_egress.prompt_en: allowed to send data to the listed destinations

credentials.description: The provider needs credentials the user has to supply.

write.description: The provider creates or modifies data in the target system.
write.prompt_en: allowed to write to the target system

destructive.description: The provider removes or overwrites data that existed before it ran.
destructive.prompt_en: allowed to delete or overwrite existing data

deployment.description: The provider changes what is running in an environment.
deployment.prompt_en: allowed to deploy to the target environment

external_accounts.description: The provider acts in a third-party account: a registry, a mail provider, a cloud console.
external_accounts.prompt_en: allowed to act in the named external accounts

metered_cost.description: Running the provider spends money or metered quota.
metered_cost.prompt_en: allowed to spend the stated budget

effects.read_rule: Reading a local working tree is not an effect that needs authorization: the user pointed the review at it. Reading a deployed system is, and it appears here as network plus data_egress.

control_not_covered.description: The provider makes no claim about this control at all.

operation_not_covered.description: The provider covers the control but not the requested operations or actors.

subject_not_covered.description: The provider cannot observe this kind of subject.

target_unavailable.description: The thing the provider needs to observe is not part of this application: no Supabase project, no deployed URL, no source tree.

environment_unsupported.description: The provider cannot produce an observation about the environment being assessed. Observations never travel between environments, so this excludes it outright.

authorization_scope_mismatch.description: This run was authorized for one environment and the requirement is about another. Permission to probe the staging project is not permission to probe production, and an observation made in staging says nothing about production either way. Both halves of that fail at once, so a provider that acts on a live system is excluded outright rather than quietly re-pointed.

tool_unavailable.description: The provider is not bundled and the tools it needs are not installed here.

executor_unavailable.description: Nobody who could run this method is available for this review.

credentials_missing.description: The provider needs credentials that have not been supplied.

input_missing.description: The provider needs an input or data fixture that has not been supplied: a known private record, a base URL, a documented flow.

prerequisite_unmet.description: A stated precondition for running the provider at all has not been met. Prerequisites are prose for a person, so this is raised only when the caller names one it knows to be unmet; the machine-checkable half of every prerequisite lives in required_targets, required_inputs, availability or authorization, and is checked there.

authorization_not_granted.description: The provider declares that it requires authorization and none was given for this run.

network_not_accepted.description: The provider reaches the network and network access was not authorized.

data_egress_not_accepted.description: The provider sends data out, or sends it to a destination that was not authorized.

side_effect_not_authorized.description: Covering the requested cells would require a write, destructive, deployment or external-account effect that was not authorized.

cost_not_accepted.description: The provider's monetary or compute cost is above what was accepted, or is unknown while only known costs were accepted.

selection.rule: Prefer the strongest applicable method whose authorization, environment, credential, cost, egress and side-effect requirements have actually been accepted for this run. Rank every applicable provider, walk the ranking, and add a provider to the plan while it still contributes a requested cell nothing earlier in the plan covers. Stop when the requested cells are exhausted or the ranking is. Nothing that was excluded disappears: an excluded provider that a user could have enabled is reported with the exact reason and the exact grant that would have enabled it.

rank_keys.rationale: An observation of the running system is worth more than a reading of its source, whatever the source says. This is the same rule that refuses static analysis a coverage cell.
Within one kind of observation, prefer the method that can settle its claim over the method that only produces material for a human.

The declared preference between methods of equal strength: cheapest and least intrusive first, which for authorization means the API probe before a browser flow before a person. Maintained specialist tools rank ahead of the human review and the bundled grep scanner, because a tool that costs nothing to run and was written by people who do only this finds more than either — and behind the live methods, because reading the source is still not watching the deployment. A person reading the code stays ahead of the bundled scanner, where it has always been.
A total order. Two providers that tie on everything above still have to rank in the same order every time, or the plan stops being reproducible.

selection.determinism_rule: The rank keys are a total order over any set of capabilities, and the plan is built by a single pass over that order. The same requirement and the same available capabilities therefore produce the same plan, in the same order, with the same explanation, regardless of the order the capabilities were loaded in.
selection.gap_rule: A provider excluded for a reason whose constraint kind records a coverage gap is a gap, never a silent skip. The gap names the provider, the constraint, and what would resolve it, and it stays visible in the plan even when a weaker provider was selected in its place.
selection.authorization_rule: A plan step whose provider declares an effect that requires authorization is not an instruction to run: it is a request. The request names the exact provider, the exact effects, the destinations data would reach, the credentials needed and the cost, and the run may not start until that exact request has been granted.
selection.authorization_scope_rule: An authorization is granted for one environment and holds only there. When the offer names a different environment from the requirement, every provider that acts on a live system — one that requires authorization, reaches the network, or has an effect beyond reading — is excluded, because using the grant would both stretch it to a scope nobody approved and produce an observation about the wrong environment. A provider that only reads the source the review was already pointed at is not acting in an environment at all, so the mismatch does not touch it: it stays the last resort of the chain, indicative as always.
selection.closure_rule: Selection covers cells; it never closes controls. A plan that covers every requested cell has established the requirement it was given, which is a smaller statement than the control. Whether the control closes is decided by the coverage model and the assessment rules (R3, R4, R20) against evidence that actually exists, not by a plan that says the evidence could exist.
selection.no_conclusion_rule: A provider produces Evidence, with a direction and a strength and a stated scope. It never writes an assessment, a control status or a readiness state. A provider that could produce a conclusion could be pointed at a control and asked for a pass, which is the failure mode this whole model exists to prevent.

providers.name: vibecheck Supabase live probe
providers.summary_en: Sends real requests to the deployed Supabase project with the public key and, when two test-account tokens are supplied, reads one account's record with the other account's session.

availability.detect: Bundled with vibecheck; needs no installation.

coverage.closure_threshold: One cell per request: this table, an anonymous caller, a read, this environment. The control closes only when every required cell of the matrix has been observed denied in the assessed environment.
One anonymous insert into one table. It is opt-in because a successful one leaves a real row behind, and the attempt owns its cleanup.
One known record, read by one unrelated account. Cross-account create, update and delete are not automated here and stay open until another provider records them.

authorization.notes: Refuses service_role keys outright. Write probing is opt-in per run and records the row it created and the state of its cleanup.

required_inputs.description: The publishable/anon key the browser already ships.
A session token for a first test account, used to establish that a record exists.
A session token for a second, unrelated test account.
The identifier of a record account A owns, so a refusal for account B is a denial rather than an empty result.

prerequisites: The project owner authorizes probing this project, which is what authorization.required records.

targets: the Supabase project URL supplied for the run

destinations: the Supabase project URL supplied for the run

confidence.limitations: Zero visible rows means row level security or an empty table, and the difference is settled by reading the same window as a test account rather than assumed. It sees PostgREST; an application route in front of the database is a separate question.

evidence_freshness.typical_validity: until the next migration or policy change

providers.name: Playwright two-account flow
providers.summary_en: A scripted browser signs in as two unrelated test accounts and tries to reach each other's records through the real application, including the routes and server code the database probe never sees.
providers.mechanism: playwright test project maintained alongside the application

availability.detect: Not bundled with vibecheck. Available when a Playwright project with two-account fixtures exists in the repository and its browsers are installed.

coverage.closure_threshold: One route, one actor, one operation per assertion. The flow closes exactly the cells its assertions name.
One write attempt per named route. A write that reaches validation already refutes the claim; a write that is refused closes that one cell.
A delete attempt against a record that exists. It is separately opt-in because a successful one removes data that was there before the review started.
One record of account A, requested through the application as account B.
One modification of account A's record attempted as account B.
One deletion of account A's record attempted as account B.
One shared record of tenant A, requested as a member of tenant B.
One write into tenant A's scope attempted as a member of tenant B.
One deletion in tenant A's scope attempted as a member of tenant B.
One privileged route requested from an account that does not hold the role, with the client-side navigation bypassed.
One privileged write attempted from an account without the role.
One privileged deletion attempted from an account without the role.

An undeclared route observed refusing an unauthenticated request is evidence about that route. Default-deny is a statement about every route, including the ones nobody wrote a test for, so a flow cannot close it.

The flows a maintained suite asserts on, observed passing against this deployment. A suite that covers the sign-up path says nothing about checkout, so closure needs the critical flows named first and then asserted.

Automated cross-account assertions exist and ran against this deployment. What each assertion establishes about authorization itself is a coverage cell, tracked separately from whether the tests exist at all.

credentials: two test-account logins for the deployment under test
authorization.notes: Drives the real application. Read-only assertions are safe against a shared environment; create, update and delete assertions leave data behind and are separately opt-in.

required_inputs.description: The URL of the deployment the flow runs against.
Credentials for a first test account.
Credentials for a second, unrelated test account.
The maintained Playwright project naming the routes and records each assertion uses. Without it there is nothing to run.

prerequisites: A Playwright project with two-account fixtures exists and its browsers are installed, which availability.requires_tools and the two_account_flow_spec input record.
The deployment owner authorizes automated traffic against it, which authorization.required records.

cost.notes: Free to run and expensive to write: the flows are application-specific and have to be maintained alongside the routes they assert on.

targets: the deployment base URL supplied for the run

destinations: the deployment base URL supplied for the run

confidence.limitations: It tests the routes somebody wrote an assertion for. An unasserted route is not a passing route, and a flow that signs in through the UI can be defeated by an unrelated UI change rather than by an authorization failure.

run_semantics.timeout: Playwright's own per-test timeout. A timed-out assertion observed no decision by the application and is imported as an inconclusive cell, never as a refusal.
run_semantics.cancellation: Safe for read-only assertions. A cancelled write or delete flow may leave test data behind, which is why those assertions are separately opt-in.
run_semantics.partial_results: The reporter writes the assertions that ran; the ones that did not stay uncovered and are not a pass.
run_semantics.failure: A browser that will not launch or a sign-in that fails produces no evidence and one open verify Action. A failed assertion is a result, not a failure.

providers.name: Guided two-account browser test
providers.summary_en: A person signs in as two test accounts in an ordinary browser, follows a written script, and records what each account could and could not reach.
providers.mechanism: documented manual steps with a recorded result

availability.detect: Always available to a review with a person in it and two usable test accounts; executor_role records that the person is the requirement.

coverage.closure_threshold: One page or link opened in a private window, on one object. What the person saw is the observation; 'it looked fine' is not one.
One record's URL, created by account A and opened by account B. The record has to be one account A can actually see, or a blank page proves nothing.
One shared record's URL, opened by a member of the other organisation.
One admin URL typed directly into the address bar from an ordinary account. A hidden menu item is not an enforced check.

credentials: two test accounts on the deployment
authorization.notes: Read-only by design. The script never asks anyone to create, change or delete data in an environment other people are using.

required_inputs.description: The address of a record account A can see, so account B's result means something.

prerequisites: Someone is available to run the steps and write down what happened, which executor_role records.

cost.notes: Roughly fifteen minutes per object type, every time it has to be repeated. That recurring cost is the argument for automating it, not a reason to skip it now.

confidence.limitations: It covers what the script names and what the person actually did. Steps get skipped, results get remembered rather than recorded, and nobody repeats it after the next deploy.

providers.name: Code and policy review
providers.summary_en: A person who can read the application reads the authorization policies, the server routes and the queries, and states what the source intends.
providers.mechanism: guided reading of the source and configuration

availability.detect: Available whenever the source is available and somebody can read it. This is the last resort of the chain, and it is never empty.

coverage_rules.closure_threshold: Closes nothing about the deployed system. A policy that exists in the repository may be unapplied, overridden in a dashboard, or shadowed by a second data path; source and deployment look identical from here. It is the strongest thing available when nobody may touch the running system, and the weakest thing available when they may.

authorization.notes: Reads what the review was already pointed at.

prerequisites: Someone who can read the application's source is available, which executor_role records.
providers.environments_note: A source reading is material about whichever environment runs that source, which is why this provider is the last resort of the chain in every environment rather than only in the developer's own. It stays indicative and fills no cell there, because the deployed policy and the committed one look identical from here.

confidence.limitations: Reading is not running. It finds what is written down, in the files the reader opened, and says nothing about configuration held outside the repository.

providers.name: vibecheck SQL migration analysis
providers.summary_en: Recognizes table creation and row-level-security statements in committed migrations and reports the tables created without a matching policy.

availability.detect: Bundled with vibecheck; runs when the repository contains SQL migrations.

coverage.closure_threshold: Closes nothing. Migrations state what the source intends, and an unapplied migration, a dashboard override and an applied one all look the same from here.
Closes nothing, for the same reason. A table created without row level security is material worth acting on; it is not an observation of the deployment.
Closes nothing. A policy expression matching every row is material about who can reach which record, and whether that is intended is a decision rather than a signal.

prerequisites: The repository contains SQL migrations, which required_targets records.
providers.environments_note: Committed migrations are material about whatever environment they were applied to, and about none of them conclusively: an unapplied migration and an applied one are the same text. Indicative everywhere, a cell nowhere.

confidence.limitations: Statement recognition, not a SQL parser. Policies applied outside migrations are invisible to it, and a policy that exists can still be wrong.

providers.name: vibecheck.sh static scanner
providers.summary_en: Regex and path heuristics over the working tree. Emits WARN, NO_SIGNAL or MANUAL per check; it proves neither a vulnerability nor its absence.

availability.detect: Bundled with vibecheck; needs no installation.

coverage_rules.closure_threshold: Closes nothing. A match is material for a reviewer and a non-match is the absence of a match, which is not the absence of the problem: NO_SIGNAL is never a pass.

authorization.notes: Reads the working tree. The optional advisory lookup is the only part that leaves the machine and it is off unless asked for.

providers.environments_note: The working tree is the source of whatever is deployed, so a match is material for every environment that runs it. It is never more than material: the scanner has no view of the running system at all.

confidence.limitations: Path and pattern heuristics with no dataflow and no type information. Every hit needs a reviewer, and the checks it has no rule for are emitted as explicit to-dos rather than passed over.

providers.name: Gitleaks secret scanner
providers.summary_en: Pattern and entropy rules run over the commits a reviewer points them at, including credentials that were deleted from the working tree and are still in the history.

availability.detect: Available when a `gitleaks` executable is on PATH. vibecheck never installs it: an absent tool is a recorded coverage gap, and what runs on the user's machine is the user's decision.

coverage.closure_threshold: A clean run over the *whole* history, plus the reviewer's confirmation that the scanned range is the whole history. A default run reads the working tree only, which is the one case where a green result means least.
A provider key rule that fires is a finding about that key. Nothing closes here: a rule that did not fire has not established that no provider key ships to the client.
A hit in a file that ships to the browser is a finding about that file. The control speaks about the built bundle, which this never reads.

authorization.notes: Reads the local repository and writes a report file where the caller asks for one.

prerequisites: The review has a git repository with history, not an exported snapshot.
providers.environments_note: It reads a working tree, so it is not acting in an environment at all; the environment on its evidence is the one the source belongs to.

cost.notes: Free. Triaging its output is not: entropy rules fire on test fixtures and generated files.

confidence.limitations: Regex and entropy, not semantics. It finds credential shapes it has a rule for, in the revisions it was pointed at; a passphrase, an unusual key format or an unscanned branch is a miss, and a green run is never a control-wide pass.

run_semantics.timeout: Caller-imposed. A history scan of a large repository is minutes, not seconds; the adapter applies no timeout of its own.
run_semantics.cancellation: Safe at any point: the run only reads. A cancelled run imports as a partial result with an open verify Action.
run_semantics.partial_results: Findings written before the run stopped are evidence about themselves; the commits it never reached stay uncovered.
run_semantics.failure: A non-zero exit means findings, not an error. A crash or an unreadable report produces no evidence and one open verify Action.

providers.name: TruffleHog credential scanner
providers.summary_en: Credential detectors over git history, with optional live verification against the provider each candidate belongs to.
providers.mechanism: trufflehog git file://<repo> --json --no-update (add --only-verified to trade recall for precision; verification is what makes the run reach the network)

availability.detect: Available when a `trufflehog` executable is on PATH. Never installed by vibecheck.

coverage.closure_threshold: A clean run over the whole history. A verified hit is the strongest signal available here — the credential was live at scan time — and it still describes that credential, not the control.
A detector that fires is a finding about that provider's key. Nothing closes on a detector that stayed silent.
A hit in a file that ships to the browser is a finding about that file, not about the built bundle.

authorization.notes: Reads the local repository. Verification sends the candidate credential to the provider that issued it, which is a network call and an egress of the credential itself — it is opt-in for that reason.

prerequisites: The review has a git repository with history.
providers.environments_note: It reads a working tree, so it is not acting in an environment at all.

targets: the issuing provider of each candidate credential, when verification is enabled

destinations: the issuing provider of each candidate credential, when verification is enabled

confidence.limitations: Detector-based. Verification removes most false positives for the providers it supports and does nothing for the ones it does not; an unsupported credential type is a miss either way.

run_semantics.timeout: Caller-imposed. Verification adds a network round trip per candidate.
run_semantics.cancellation: Safe at any point: read-only against the local clone.
run_semantics.partial_results: The JSON-lines stream is imported line by line, so a stopped run keeps what it emitted; lines that do not parse are counted and reported rather than dropped in silence.
run_semantics.failure: No readable line produces no evidence and one open verify Action.

providers.name: OSV-Scanner dependency audit
providers.summary_en: Declared dependency versions are matched against the OSV advisory database.

availability.detect: Available when an `osv-scanner` executable is on PATH. Never installed by vibecheck.

coverage.closure_threshold: A clean audit of every lockfile the application actually ships, on a date a reviewer records. Advisories are published continuously, so a clean run is a statement about a moment, not a property of the project.
Nothing here closes it. An advisory lookup says nothing about who publishes a package, whether the name is a typosquat, or whether it was pinned deliberately.

authorization.notes: Reads local manifests and queries the OSV API. The dependency names and versions of the project leave the machine as part of the lookup.

prerequisites: A lockfile or manifest the tool supports exists in the repository.
providers.environments_note: It reads declared dependencies, not a deployment; the environment on its evidence is the one the source belongs to.

confidence.limitations: It reports advisories against declared versions. It does not know whether the vulnerable code path is reachable from this application, and it cannot see a dependency that is vendored, unpinned or installed outside the lockfile.

run_semantics.timeout: Caller-imposed. The run is a lookup against a remote API and fails the way a network call fails.
run_semantics.cancellation: Safe at any point: no local or remote state changes.
run_semantics.partial_results: Advisories returned before the stop are imported; lockfiles never read stay uncovered.
run_semantics.failure: An unreachable database or an unreadable lockfile produces no evidence and one open verify Action — an audit that could not run is not a clean audit.

providers.name: Trivy dependency, image and licence scanner
providers.summary_en: Filesystem, lockfile and container-image layers are matched against vulnerability and licence databases.
providers.mechanism: trivy fs --format json --scanners vuln,license <path>, or trivy image --format json <image>

availability.detect: Available when a `trivy` executable is on PATH. Never installed by vibecheck.

coverage.closure_threshold: A clean scan of the artifacts that actually ship — the image as well as the lockfile — on a recorded date.
The licence inventory is material for a decision about how this application is distributed. Compatibility is that decision, and no scanner makes it.
Nothing here closes it: the scan reports known advisories, not the provenance of a package.

authorization.notes: Reads the filesystem or image layers and downloads its vulnerability database. Scanning a private image needs whatever credentials that registry requires.

prerequisites: A supported lockfile, filesystem path or container image is available to scan.
providers.environments_note: It reads build artifacts, not a running deployment.

confidence.limitations: Severity is the advisory's, not this application's. Image scanning sees the layers it was given, and a base image rebuilt since the scan is a different artifact.

run_semantics.timeout: Caller-imposed. The first run also downloads the vulnerability database.
run_semantics.cancellation: Safe at any point: read-only against the filesystem or image layers.
run_semantics.partial_results: Results per target are imported as they were written; targets never reached stay uncovered.
run_semantics.failure: A stale or undownloadable database is a failure, not a clean scan, and produces one open verify Action.

providers.name: Semgrep Community Edition
providers.summary_en: Rule-based static analysis with intra-file dataflow over the source, for injection classes, unsafe rendering and framework misconfiguration.
providers.mechanism: semgrep scan --config auto --json --metrics=off (--config auto fetches the registry ruleset; --config <local dir> keeps the run offline)

availability.detect: Available when a `semgrep` executable is on PATH. Never installed by vibecheck.

coverage.closure_threshold: A confirmed hit is a finding about that query. A clean run over a language and framework the ruleset actually supports is material; the control closes when a reviewer has seen how queries are built, not when a rule stayed quiet.
Unsafe rendering sinks the ruleset recognizes. A template system it has no rules for is unscanned, not clean.
Command, path, SSRF, XXE and deserialization sinks the ruleset recognizes, in the files it parsed.
Nothing closes it here. Whether every server entry point validates its input is a statement about routes nobody wrote a rule for as much as the ones somebody did.
A debug flag in committed configuration is a finding about the source. What the deployment runs is a live observation this never makes.
A model response reaching an execution sink in one file. The rules are intra-file, so a path that crosses a module boundary is a miss.

authorization.notes: Reads the working tree. `--config auto` fetches rules from the Semgrep registry, which is a network call; a local ruleset keeps the run offline. Source code is not uploaded in either case.

prerequisites: Source in a language the chosen ruleset supports.
providers.environments_note: It reads a working tree, so it is not acting in an environment at all.

cost.notes: Community Edition is free. Triage is where the time goes.

targets: the Semgrep rule registry, when the ruleset is fetched rather than local

confidence.limitations: Syntactic patterns with intra-file dataflow. It does not follow taint across files or through a framework's dispatch, and it reads the source rather than the deployment, so it can never fill an authorization coverage cell.

run_semantics.timeout: Semgrep's own per-rule and per-file timeouts. Files it gave up on appear in the run's error list and are imported as a gap.
run_semantics.cancellation: Safe at any point: read-only against the working tree.
run_semantics.partial_results: Results collected before the stop are imported; the rules and files not reached stay uncovered.
run_semantics.failure: Unparseable output produces no evidence and one open verify Action. A rule that maps to no declared control becomes a triage Action rather than a claim.

providers.name: Codex Security
providers.summary_en: An LLM security scanner that maps the codebase, hunts for vulnerabilities across components, adversarially validates each finding, and returns structured findings with file and line locations that can be exported as SARIF.
providers.mechanism: npx @openai/codex-security (local tree scan; validated findings return as findings.json/SARIF; an opt-in send mode runs model-side validation using the caller's authenticated session)

availability.detect: Available when a `codex-security` executable is on PATH or reachable via `npx @openai/codex-security`. Never installed by vibecheck.

coverage.closure_threshold: A traced path from an untrusted source to a query sink, as found and adversarially validated by the LLM. A clean run over the language and framework it supports is material; the control closes when a reviewer has seen how queries are built, not when a model stayed quiet.
A traced path from an untrusted source to a rendering sink.
A traced path to a command, path, SSRF or deserialization sink.
Nothing closes it here: an unqueried entry point is not a validated one.
A debug flag in committed configuration is a finding about the source. What the deployment runs is a live observation this never makes.
A model response reaching an execution sink, followed across files by the model and validated. A path it did not complete is a miss; no source reading is a deployment observation.

authorization.notes: Reads the working tree. The opt-in send mode may send source excerpts to the model endpoint through the caller's authenticated session; a local run and a send-enabled run behave differently, and neither uploads to vibecheck-controlled infrastructure. A finding it validated is still evidence a reviewer confirms, never a control-wide conclusion.

prerequisites: Source in a language Codex Security's model can reason about.
providers.environments_note: It reads a working tree, so it is not acting in an environment at all; the environment on its evidence is the one the source belongs to.

cost.notes: The SDK and local CLI are free to use; a validation-enabled run may consume model tokens. Triaging reported findings is where the time goes.

targets: the OpenAI model endpoint, only when the run sends source excerpts for validation or triage

destinations: the OpenAI endpoint the caller's authenticated session is configured to reach, only when the opt-in send mode is on

confidence.limitations: A strong cross-file reader, but still a source reader. It reports what is written and what it reasoned from; it cannot observe the deployment, and a clean run never proves a control-wide absence.

run_semantics.timeout: Caller-imposed. A deep model scan and its validation take minutes on a large codebase; no scanner-provided timeout is enforced.
run_semantics.cancellation: Safe at any point in the local scan; a cancelled run imports as a partial result with an open verify Action.
run_semantics.partial_results: Findings written before the stop are evidence about themselves; the files and paths never reached stay uncovered.
run_semantics.failure: A crash, timeout or unparseable output produces no evidence and one open verify Action. A validated finding is triaged, never treated as proof.

providers.name: CodeQL semantic analysis
providers.summary_en: Interprocedural taint tracking over a compiled analysis database, following untrusted input to sinks across files.
providers.mechanism: codeql database create <db> --language=<lang> && codeql database analyze <db> <suite> --format=sarif-latest --output=<file>

availability.detect: Available when a `codeql` executable is on PATH and the project builds. Free for open-source repositories; a licence question for private ones, which is the user's to answer before it runs.

coverage.closure_threshold: A traced path from an untrusted source to a query sink. A clean suite over a language it fully supports is the strongest static material available here and still not a live observation.
A traced path from an untrusted source to a rendering sink.
A traced path to a command, path, SSRF or deserialization sink.
Nothing closes it here: an unqueried entry point is not a validated one.

authorization.notes: Reads the source and builds an analysis database in a scratch directory of the caller's choosing. That database is a build artifact, not a change to the application under review, which is why no write effect is declared. Nothing is uploaded unless the caller chooses to publish the SARIF to a code-scanning service, which is a separate step this registry does not perform.

prerequisites: The project builds, or the language is one CodeQL can extract without a build.
The repository's licence terms permit CodeQL analysis; free for open source, otherwise the user's decision.
providers.environments_note: It reads source, so it is not acting in an environment at all.

cost.notes: Database creation dominates: minutes to hours on a large codebase, which is why it ranks below Semgrep despite finding more.

confidence.limitations: Deep for the languages and query suites it supports and blind outside them. It reads source, not the deployment, so it can never fill an authorization coverage cell.

run_semantics.timeout: Caller-imposed. Database creation dominates and is minutes to hours on a large codebase.
run_semantics.cancellation: Safe at any point; the analysis database is a build artifact and can be discarded.
run_semantics.partial_results: SARIF is written at the end of a query suite, so a cancelled analysis usually yields nothing rather than a partial file.
run_semantics.failure: A failed build step means no database and therefore no result: an open verify Action, never a clean report.

providers.name: OWASP ZAP baseline scan
providers.summary_en: A scanner crawls an authorized deployment and reports what its responses, headers and error pages give away.
providers.mechanism: zap-baseline.py -t <authorized target URL> -J <report.json> (passive baseline; -a enables the active scan and needs its own authorization)

availability.detect: Available when ZAP is installed or its container image is present. Never installed by vibecheck.

coverage.closure_threshold: HSTS, redirect and cookie-flag behaviour on the routes the spider reached. Routes it did not reach are unscanned, not secure.
The Access-Control-Allow-Origin behaviour observed on the routes it reached.
Stack traces, debug endpoints and verbose headers returned by this deployment, as observed.
Reflected content and missing response-header protections on the routes it reached. The passive baseline does not attempt injection.
Only the active scan sends malformed input, and it needs its own authorization. Nothing here closes the control.

A route that returns data to an unauthenticated crawler is a finding about that route. It fills no coverage cell: the crawler has no second account to compare against and no idea which object it just read, which is exactly what a cell has to name.

authorization.notes: Sends traffic at somebody's deployment. It runs against an explicitly authorized non-production target with a resolved scope; a production run is a separate approval, and the active scan is a third.

required_inputs.description: The exact deployment URL authorized for this scan. Evidence that cannot name its target is not importable.
Who authorized the scan of that target, recorded with the evidence.

prerequisites: The target is a non-production deployment, or a production run has been separately approved.
The owner of the target has authorized automated traffic against it and the scope is resolved.

targets: the authorized target URL supplied for the run

destinations: the authorized target URL supplied for the run

side_effects.details: The baseline profile is passive: it crawls and reads. The active scan sends crafted input and can create, modify or corrupt data, which is why it is a separate opt-in.

confidence.limitations: It reports on the routes its spider found, unauthenticated unless it was given a session. An application behind a login is largely invisible to a baseline run, and a quiet report mostly means the crawler did not get in.

run_semantics.timeout: Caller-imposed, and a scan against somebody's deployment should have one. The baseline profile is passive and bounded by the spider.
run_semantics.cancellation: Safe at any point for the passive profile. A cancelled active scan may leave the target with partially processed input.
run_semantics.partial_results: Alerts raised before the stop are imported; routes the spider never reached stay uncovered, which is the usual case and is stated in every evidence scope.
run_semantics.failure: Exit codes 1 and 2 are alert levels, not errors. An unreachable target produces no evidence and one open verify Action.
